content.text: let's review this PR, https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1009 on top of 993, which improves a few things, most notably adding a prompt to review. In 993, we did add message which lets the user know what was being reviewed, which by default is everything on branch since review started agent session. Now user can input prompt and is stored. There are a few other problems. 1. picker doens't prompt installatation if the skill isn't installed, so we have barrier here. we could either only include skills that are installe with the agent, parse subdirectory and lists all skills you have and everything that has review in it, or something else, 2. if you have both codex, cluade, or any other agents installed, onyl claude starts, we need a way to make this better UI so user can either select which agent to use, verify agent flag, (but also better UI), 2b. user also needs to be able to spawn both/multiple agents simultaneously, so user can see all agents at the same time. sort of like how the pr-review-toolkit does when it spawns its subagents you see each one, spinning, you can also have the option to cntrl + o to open and see more details, then at the end maybe take everything and aggregate and summarize everything to user then could also attach. - use /superpowers:brainstorming and take your time with these two from 1009 which are improvements to 993. So first evaluate 1009 and then these, with what is most updated on cli main
I'll start by pulling PR #1009 details and comparing to current main, then use `/superpowers:brainstorming` for the improvement ideas. Let me gather context first.

A few review / bug fixes.

- removed `--track-only` replaced it with `entire review attach` instead - I think `--track-only` is to complicated and easy to forget (both to do it before, but also to remove it after)
- allow specifying a "prompt" instead of just using skills (is not great yet, the page after the skill pick asks you for a prompt)

```
  {
    "review": {
      "claude-code": {
        "skills": ["/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr", "/test-auditor"],
        "prompt": "Focus on security regressions this week, then run the skills above."
      }
    }
  }
```

- `--agent <name>` flag (`47c40ada2`) — select a specific configured agent when more than one is in `review:`; unknown value surfaces a concrete error listing the configured alternatives.

- Hooks-installed gate(`d420e6671`) — aborts with a clear `entire configure --agent <name>` pointer when the selected agent's hooks aren't installed (silent failure shape: marker would otherwise be written with no hook to adopt it).

- `ReviewPrompt` field (`7d9aadb91`) — records the ground-truth text of the review request alongside the structured `ReviewSkills` list. Composed prompt for spawn; first user prompt from the transcript for attach.

- Review-attach surfaces (`2505c5fd2`) — two equivalent ways to tag an existing session as a review:

```
entire attach <session-id> --review [--skills "/a,/b"]
entire review attach <session-id> [--skills "/a,/b"]
```

Both funnel into `runAttach` via an `attachOptions` struct. Skills resolve after agent detection (`d81953ed5`) so a Gemini session attached without `--agent` correctly auto-detects. External agents work on both surfaces (`76535a29d`).

This also adds the first prompt from the log as review_prompt


### UX polish

**First-run banner** (`7f2fdb06b`) — running `entire review` with no config used to silently drop into the picker. Now prints an explicit "first-run setup" banner, gates the picker on a huh confirmation, and signposts "Setup complete — running review now." when transitioning to the actual review.

**Helpful error text** in the empty-installed-agents case.

### Internal cleanups

- `runAttach` grew an `attachOptions` struct to avoid a 6th positional param.
- Extracted `runAttachSurfaceReviewErrors` so review-mode errors reach stderr under root's `SilenceErrors=true`.
- `review_test.go` got a shared `setupReviewTestRepoWithCommit` helper, test constants for repeated agent/skill names, and a `reflect.DeepEqual` merge-result assertion fixing a bug where multi-element skill slices weren't compared element-wise.
- `slices.Contains` replaces a throwaway map build in the hooks gate; direct map lookup replaces a linear scan in `selectReviewAgent`'s override path.

### Test coverage

- Regression tests for every correctness fix (marker agent/SHA binding, picker wipes, fallback marker survival, existing-checkpoint review refusal).
- End-to-end integration tests for both attach surfaces, including Gemini auto-detection without `--agent`.
- Pinned behavior tests for the data model: `ReviewPrompt` roundtrip, marker location, `Kind.IsReview` umbrella, config-doesn't-leak-into-attach.

All unit + integration + canary E2E tests green. No API calls consumed — Vogon canary + external-agent canary cover the checkpointing paths.

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes the persisted review configuration schema and checkpoint/session metadata (adds `review_prompt`), plus modifies review marker adoption logic; this can affect backward compatibility and how reviews are tagged/recorded across agents and repos.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **review-mode attach** support via `entire attach --review` (plus new `entire review attach` alias), recording review metadata (`kind=agent_review`, optional `review_skills`, and new **`review_prompt`** captured from the transcript’s first user prompt) into session state and committed checkpoint metadata.
>

Extensive new unit/integration tests cover these regressions and end-to-end flows.

Entire-Checkpoint: 5e2acf066b8b","messageHeadline":"Preserve uncurated review config entries on --edit","oid":"c2961fe4b9149bafbbbf8b74a4d4a19e8cc2ec5e"},{"authoredDate":"2026-04-22T12:01:59Z","authors":[{"email":"stefan@entire.io","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjcwNzQx","login":"Soph","name":"Stefan Haubold"},{"email":"noreply@anthropic.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjgxODQ3","login":"claude","name":"Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context)"}],"committedDate":"2026-04-22T12:01:59Z","messageBody":"PendingReviewMarker records StartingSHA at marker-write time, but
adoptPendingReviewMarkerInto never consulted it. The failure mode:

  1. User runs 'entire review --track-only' at SHA A, intending to
     review SHA A's code.
  2. User commits (HEAD moves to SHA B) without starting the review.
  3. Later, an unrelated agent session starts in the same worktree.
  4. The session's UserPromptSubmit hook claims the stale marker and
     tags an unrelated session as a review of code that already moved on.

On adoption, compare current HEAD to StartingSHA. Mismatched SHA
indicates the user's original intent no longer applies: clear the
stale marker (so it can't mis-tag future sessions either) and do not
adopt. Unlike worktree/agent mismatches — which leave the marker for
the correct session to claim — a SHA mismatch can never resolve, so
clearing is the safe default.

Failure to resolve HEAD is non-fatal; log at Debug and skip the check.

Here's my PR #1009 evaluation — then I'll pivot to `/superpowers:brainstorming` for your two improvement ideas.

## PR #1009 — review pass

**Scope**: +1530/-162 across 16 files on top of PR #993 (`feat/entire-review`). Net changes:
1. `Review` settings shape: `map[string][]string` → `map[string]ReviewConfig{Skills, Prompt}` — unlocks the custom-prompt UX you called out.
2. `--track-only` removed; replaced with `entire review attach` + `entire attach --review`.
3. `--agent NAME` flag for picking among configured agents.
4. Hooks-installed gate: aborts if the selected agent's hooks aren't installed.
5. Marker adoption scoping upgraded from `(worktree)` to `(worktree, agent, starting-SHA)`.
6. `ReviewPrompt` field persisted end-to-end (session state + both v1/v2 committed metadata).

### Strengths

- **Silent-failure hunting is real this time.** The `--agent mismatch` error lists alternatives (`review.go:691`), the hooks gate errors with the exact `entire configure` command to run (`review.go:625`), and the non-launchable-agent path rearranges the cleanup defer *after* `LauncherFor` so a cursor fallback doesn't silently wipe its own marker (`review.go:633-643`). The regression test `TestRunReview_NonLaunchableAgentPreservesMarker` locks that in.
- **Marker scoping thinks through "what if multiple sessions race."** Worktree match + agent match + SHA freshness, each with a comment explaining why that specific mismatch is left-in-place vs. cleared. The SHA-stale case is rightly cleared (no future session will match), while wrong-agent is left in place (correct agent may still arrive). This is the kind of distinction most PRs gloss over.
- **`resolveReviewSkills` for attach refuses to silently pull from config.** Comment: "Silently attaching configured skills would misrepresent the session as having run skills it may not have." That's a load-bearing design call — the review record is a factual claim, and the author picks ground-truth over ergonomics.
- **`mergePickerResults` pins a data-loss bug with a test.** External/uncurated entries the picker can't surface survive `--edit`; previously they'd silently disappear.
- **Integration tests cover the three hardest cases.** Full adoption → condensation loop, wrong-agent leaves marker, stale SHA clears it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The marker adoption logic is a **three-key filter** (worktree, agent, SHA) but each key has *different* semantics on mismatch: worktree/agent leave the marker for a later legitimate claim; SHA clears it because no future session could legitimately match. Encoding "leave vs. clear" per-dimension is more nuanced than a typical gate and worth preserving as a principle if more dimensions appear later.
- `runAttachSurfaceReviewErrors` is an interesting pattern — a wrapper that re-routes error formatting based on `opts.Review`. It's a small leak of surface concerns into the business function, but the alternative (threading a `cobra.Command` into `runAttach` just for `SilenceUsage`) is worse.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

### Issues found

**🔴 Blocking — backward-compat break in settings (both bots flagged; I confirmed).**
`EntireSettings.Review` type changed from `map[string][]string` to `map[string]ReviewConfig` with no `UnmarshalJSON` migration. `loadFromFile` uses `json.Decoder` with `DisallowUnknownFields` (and Go's default type-strict unmarshalling). A file with the old shape `{"review": {"claude-code": ["/skill"]}}` fails to decode — and because `settings.Load()` is called by **every** CLI command (lifecycle hooks, `entire enable`, etc.), the breakage is repo-wide, not scoped to `entire review`.

Saving grace: PR #993 is `OPEN` (unmerged), so no shipped release has the old shape. Risk:
- Anyone who tested `feat/entire-review` locally and persisted an old-shape config.
- If 993 merges first and 1009 later, any user who runs `entire review --edit` in between will persist old-shape settings and break on the next upgrade.

**Fix options** (pick one):
- (a) Land 993+1009 as a single squash/merge so no version ever ships the array shape.
- (b) Add `UnmarshalJSON` on `ReviewConfig` that accepts `[]string` → `{Skills: x}` or object → struct. Safer long-term.

**🟡 Non-blocking — `confirmFirstRunSetup` swallows terminal errors** (Copilot flagged).
`review.go:268` treats any `form.Run()` error as "user cancelled" and returns `false`. In headless/CI or broken-TTY environments, the command exits 0 with no review run and no diagnostic. Changing signature to `(bool, error)` preserves real failures.

**🟡 Low — stale doc comment** (Cursor flagged). `attach_test.go:838-846` has a leftover comment block describing the *opposite* of the current test behavior. 30-second cleanup.

**🟡 Minor — `confirmFirstRunSetup` is also not covered by a test**, and the non-launchable-agent path has only the "marker persists" assertion — the scoped prompt message isn't validated in detail. Nitpick-tier.

**🟢 Nice-to-have — `existing[name].Skills` indirections in picker pre-fill** (`review.go:339-340`) work correctly but read a bit thick. Could extract `savedSkillsSet(cfg ReviewConfig)` if you want. Skip if not bothering.

### Verdict

**Approve conditionally on the settings backward-compat fix.** The rest is strong — the error messaging, marker scoping, and test coverage are all material improvements over 993. Easier to ship if it lands atomically with 993.

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec review loop** — dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent with precisely crafted review context (never your session history); fix issues and re-dispatch until approved (max 5 iterations, then surface to human)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec review loop" [shape=box];
    "Spec review passed?" [shape=diamond];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec review loop";
    "Spec review loop" -> "Spec review passed?";
    "Spec review passed?" -> "Spec review loop" [label="issues found,\nfix and re-dispatch"];
    "Spec review passed?" -> "User reviews spec?" [label="approved"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Review Loop:**
After writing the spec document:

1. Dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent (see spec-document-reviewer-prompt.md)
2. If Issues Found: fix, re-dispatch, repeat until Approved
3. If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

149	// adoptPendingReviewMarkerInto reads any pending review marker and applies it
150	// to the given session state. Returns (newState, modified, error). If the
151	// state already has Kind set (e.g., a subsequent turn of a review session),
152	// the marker is left in place and modified=false — adoption only happens on
153	// first tag. The marker is cleared on successful first adoption.
154	//
155	// Worktree scoping: when the marker carries a WorktreePath, only a session
156	// whose own WorktreePath matches will adopt it. This prevents a Claude
157	// session in worktree A from racing to claim a marker that was meant for a
158	// session `entire review` just launched in worktree B (both worktrees share
159	// the same .git/entire-sessions/ directory where the marker lives).
160	// Pre-fix markers with no WorktreePath fall back to unscoped adoption.
161	func adoptPendingReviewMarkerInto(ctx context.Context, s session.State) (session.State, bool, error) {
162		// Already tagged — don't re-apply on subsequent turns.
163		if s.Kind != "" {
164			return s, false, nil
165		}
166		m, ok, err := ReadPendingReviewMarker(ctx)
167		if err != nil {

169		}
170		if !ok {
171			return s, false, nil
172		}
173		if m.WorktreePath != "" && !sameWorktreePath(m.WorktreePath, s.WorktreePath) {
174			// Marker belongs to a different worktree — leave it for the session
175			// `entire review` actually spawned, which will reach its own hook
176			// and claim the marker.
177			return s, false, nil
178		}
179		s.Kind = session.KindAgentReview
180		s.ReviewSkills = m.Skills
181		if err := ClearPendingReviewMarker(ctx); err != nil {
182			// Tagging succeeded; leftover marker self-heals on next session start
183			// (since Kind is now set, the next turn will return modified=false
184			// and the marker will be re-cleared on any next review session).
185			logging.Warn(ctx, "failed to clear pending review marker", slog.String("error", err.Error()))
186		}
187		return s, true, nil
188	}

**Question 2 (detection strategy).** Right now `curatedReviewSkills` is a hardcoded map. Four ways to know what's actually installed:

- **A. Curated ∩ installed.** Keep the hardcoded map, filter it to skills whose files exist on disk, plus runtime re-check at spawn time (warn/abort if configured skills went missing). User-authored or uncurated skills still require editing `settings.json` by hand.
- **B. Discovery-first.** Scan the agent's skill directories on disk for anything tagged or named like a review skill (e.g. `SKILL.md` frontmatter mentions "review", or filename matches). Curated map becomes a sanity-check source of descriptions, not the authoritative list.
- **C. Hybrid (my recommendation).** Show two sections in the picker: "Recommended" (curated ∩ installed, with descriptions), then "Other installed skills matching 'review'" (discovered, tagged so users know they weren't vetted). Uninstalled curated skills show up with an "install" hint instead of being hidden.
- **D. Install-on-demand.** When the user picks an uninstalled curated skill, offer to install it (agent-specific; mostly Claude Code's plugin manager). Ambitious — couples us to each agent's extension system.

**My recommendation: C, scoped tightly.** Matches your instinct from the prompt ("only include skills that are installed with the agent" + "parse subdirectory and lists all skills you have and everything that has review in it"). D is tempting but adds per-agent install plumbing I'd defer to a later spec.

Which direction do you want, or should I dig into a specific one before you decide?

for c, this part is unclear, "then "Other installed skills matching 'review'" (discovered,  
  tagged so users know they weren't vetted)", just the not vetted part. what makes a skill vetted or not

Fair — "vetted" was sloppy wording. What I actually meant:

- **Curated** = hardcoded in `curatedReviewSkills` (`review.go:126`). Someone on the entire side explicitly wrote it down with a description because we know it's a review skill: `/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr`, `/codex:adversarial-review`, etc.
- **Discovered** = any skill on disk whose name/frontmatter matches "review" but isn't on that curated list. Could be a user's personal workflow skill, a third-party marketplace skill, or just something whose name happens to contain "review" (e.g. a `/review-pull-request-format` that's really a lint rule, not a review agent).

So the gap isn't trust — it's **"does entire know this is actually a review skill, or are we guessing from a substring match?"**

Honestly, once I say it out loud, I think the distinction isn't earning its place in the UI. If a skill is installed on the user's machine, they (or their team) already decided to install it. Labeling one section "Recommended" and another "Other" just adds cognitive load.

**Revised option C':** one flat list — all skills discoverable on disk that look review-adjacent — with curated ones sorted first because we have real descriptions, and discovered ones fall below with whatever description (or filename) we can scrape. No two-tier label, no "vetted" tag.

**Question 2 (retry):** does C' read better, or do you actually want the curated/discovered distinction visible (e.g., so a user can tell "this one is official" vs "this is something my teammate wrote")?

but these skills,  Curated = hardcoded in curatedReviewSkills (review.go:126). Someone on the entire side     
  explicitly wrote it down with a description because we know it's a review skill:
  /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr, /codex:adversarial-review, etc.                                - the issue is, most people won't have these installed, vs. ones that are by default installed, is what we should change these to, and then the discover installed related to review on disk would be where these show up is what i was thinking

Got it — that reframes the whole thing. The issue isn't "curated vs discovered" as two bands in the same picker. It's that **the current curated list is full of plugin-dependent skills most users don't have installed**. Every entry in `review.go:126` except maybe `/codex:review` needs a plugin install to exist — so the picker is offering things it can't actually verify anyone has.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Skill plumbing per agent: Claude Code and Codex both separate **built-in slash commands** (ship with the agent, always present) from **plugin skills** (installed via plugin manager, live under `~/.claude/plugins/...` or `~/.codex/...`). The current curated list mixes the two and treats them the same, which is the silent-failure vector. Once we split them by install origin, "is it installed?" stops being a question about the curated list and becomes a question about the plugin directories.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Revised option C''**:

1. **Built-in shortlist** (per agent, tiny). Only skills that ship with the agent binary itself — e.g. Claude Code's `/review` if it ships built-in, `/codex:review` for Codex. These are always safe to offer.
2. **Discovered plugin skills** (per agent, variable). Walk the agent's plugin skill directories on disk, match anything whose SKILL name/description mentions review-like intent. `/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr`, `/test-auditor`, `/codex:adversarial-review`, `/superpowers:...` all land here *only if* they're installed.
3. **Nothing found?** Instead of showing an empty picker, show an inline hint: "No plugin review skills detected. Install `pr-review-toolkit` with `claude plugin install ...` to get more."

So the hardcoded map shrinks to the actually-built-in ones and becomes a safety net; everything else flows from disk discovery.

**Two follow-ups before I can commit to this:**

**Q3a** — do you want me to verify which built-in slash commands each agent actually ships with (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini), so the "built-in shortlist" is grounded in reality instead of guessed? Takes one targeted lookup per agent.

**Q3b** — for discovery, what counts as "review-related"? Options:
- **Name match** — skill name/path contains `review` (cheapest; catches `/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr`, misses `/test-auditor`).
- **Name OR description match** — also scans each `SKILL.md` frontmatter `description:` field (catches `/test-auditor` because its description says "review tests"; requires reading every skill file).
- **Explicit frontmatter tag** — require `category: review` or similar opt-in. Cleanest but needs skill authors to cooperate.

My recommendation: **Name OR description match**, case-insensitive, with keyword list `{review, audit, inspect}`. It's a small file scan, it catches the current crop of real review skills, and it doesn't require changes to anyone else's skills.

Which of 3a and 3b do you want to answer first?

Good — Q4 locked (per-agent). And you're right, 1009 didn't change picker shape; today it iterates configured agents in sequence (`review.go:244`) which reads as one unified flow but is actually per-agent under the hood. Fine as-is.

Q5 opens up a meaningful new direction. Let me split it into two decisions because they're different:

**Q5a — install pointer vs install-on-demand.**

The moment we handle Gemini (no built-in review skill at all) and Codex (only `/review`), we need *something* to fill the picker. Two ways:

- **Passive (install pointer).** When built-ins ≡ empty-ish and discovery finds nothing, picker shows a non-interactive hint line: "No review skills detected for gemini. Install with `gemini extensions install <url>` and re-run `entire review --edit`." User exits, runs the command, retries. Zero per-agent install plumbing on our side.
- **Active (install-on-demand).** Picker offers a menu: `[ ] Install gemini-review-tool now`. If selected, we shell out to the agent's own install command, then refresh discovery, then proceed. Needs a per-agent "recommended install" registry (tiny — one entry per agent) plus logic to run and verify the install succeeded.

**My lean: passive first.** Active is a smooth UX win but it creates a surface area (per-agent install command, failure modes, "the install printed an error, what do we do?") that's easy to regress. Ship passive; if users hit it often enough to complain, promote to active in a follow-up.

**Q5b — gemini scope.** Do you want gemini included in this Phase 1 spec (new curated entry = empty built-ins + install pointer to the public Gemini review tool), or left out for now and handled separately?

My lean: **include it**. If we're redesigning the picker to handle "thin built-ins + install hint," gemini is the cleanest forcing function. Leaving it out means the design is validated only against Claude (rich) and Codex (one), and we'll find out it doesn't quite fit gemini when we add it later.

## Section 2 of 3 — Discovery algorithm

### The `SkillDiscoverer` adapter, per agent

```go
// in cmd/entire/cli/agent/agent.go
type SkillDiscoverer interface {
    Agent
    DiscoverReviewSkills(ctx context.Context) ([]DiscoveredSkill, error)
}

type DiscoveredSkill struct {
    Name        string // e.g. "/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr"
    Description string // scraped from SKILL.md frontmatter if available, else ""
    SourcePath  string // disk path — for debug logging; not shown in picker
}
```

### Per-agent scan rules (what "installed" means)

| Agent | Scan root | Skill entry shape | Skill name derivation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | `~/.claude/plugins/cache/<marketplace>/<plugin>/<version>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md` + `~/.claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md` (user skills) | one directory = one skill; YAML frontmatter in SKILL.md | `/<plugin>:<skill>` for plugin skills, `/<skill>` for user skills |
| **Codex** | `~/.codex/plugins/<plugin>/` (per `/plugins` built-in) — **exact subdir layout needs a codex-rs source check before implementation; spec pins "verify before coding"** | TBD — probably `SKILL.md` or TOML manifest | `/<plugin>:<skill>` is the current Codex convention observed in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/codex/` |
| **Gemini CLI** | Gemini extensions path (TBD — needs lookup on `.gemini/extensions/` or equivalent) | per Gemini extension manifest format | `/<extension-command>` |

Implementation strategy: ship Claude Code's discoverer first (best-known layout, plus the main user base). Codex and Gemini discoverers return empty slice + nil error initially, meaning built-in + install hint is the full experience for them until their scan paths are verified. The interface is in place, so adding a real implementation later is drop-in.

### Match rule — "review-adjacent"

Case-insensitive substring match on **either** skill name **or** SKILL.md frontmatter `description:` field, against a fixed keyword set:

```go
var reviewKeywords = []string{
    "review", "audit", "inspect", "critique",
    "assess", "security-scan", "lint",
}
```

So `/test-auditor` matches on name (`audit`); `/pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter` matches on description (frontmatter says "find silent failures in code review"); `/codex:adversarial-review` matches on name.

**Why not require an explicit frontmatter tag?** Because we don't control skill authors' frontmatter, and the current crop of real review skills doesn't use one. Adding a requirement would hide skills until their authors opt in. Keyword substring catches the existing universe and doesn't gate on cooperation.

**Why cap the keyword list?** Keeps discovery predictable. Users can still manually add any skill to `settings.json` — discovery is a convenience, not a gate.

### Caching

Discovery runs only inside the picker (on `entire review` first-run or `--edit`), not on every hook fire. For a user with 50 plugin skills, worst-case scan is ~50 file reads — well under 100ms on any modern disk. No cache needed; simpler is better.

### Dedicated package or inline?

New package `cmd/entire/cli/agent/skilldiscovery/` (thin, just the interface + keyword list + match helper). Each agent package (claudecode, codex, geminicli) implements `DiscoverReviewSkills` on its agent type. Lets the review.go side import only `skilldiscovery.Matches()` and the agent adapter — no direct coupling to `~/.claude/...` paths.

### Graceful failure

`DiscoverReviewSkills` returns `(skills, error)`. Any error is logged at `Debug` and discovery is treated as "found nothing" — never blocks the picker. Concrete failure modes we plan for:

- Agent's plugin dir doesn't exist (fresh install, no plugins yet) → returns nil, nil (not an error).
- One malformed SKILL.md → skip that skill, log, continue.
- Permission error reading a plugin dir → skip, log, continue.
- Entire home directory inaccessible → returns nil, nil (benign — treat as empty).

  │
  ├─ confirmFirstRunSetup (1009) ────── user confirms? ── no ──► exit 0
  │                                         │
  │                                        yes
  ├─ runReviewConfigPicker
  │     │
  │     ├─ eligible agents := installed_and_hooked ∩ (builtins ∪ installHints)
  │     │     (NEW: gemini becomes eligible because it has an installHint)
  │     │
  │     └─ for agent in alphabetical(eligible):
  │           builtins  := curatedBuiltins[agent]
  │           disc      := agent.DiscoverReviewSkills(ctx)      ← empty if no discoverer
  │           hints     := installHints[agent] minus suppressed-by(disc)
  │           render huh.NewGroup(
  │               builtinField(builtins | noteIfEmpty),
  │               discoveredField(disc | noteIfEmpty),
  │               installHintNotes(hints),                      ← omit section if hints empty
  │               customPromptText,
  │           )
  │           cfg := ReviewConfig{
  │               Skills: dedupe(builtinPicks ++ discoveredPicks),
  │               Prompt: strings.TrimSpace(promptText),
  │           }
  │
  ├─ mergePickerResults (1009, unchanged)
  └─ save to settings.json
```

Everything below that (`selectReviewAgent`, hooks-installed gate, marker write, launcher spawn) is unchanged from 1009 **except** the new re-verification step below.

### Runtime re-verification at spawn

New guard, executed between `selectReviewAgent` and marker write in `runReview`:

```go
func verifyConfiguredSkillsInstalled(ctx context.Context, ag agent.Agent, cfg settings.ReviewConfig) error {
    if len(cfg.Skills) == 0 { return nil } // prompt-only config — nothing to verify

    builtins := curatedBuiltinNames(ag.Name())
    var discoveredNames map[string]struct{}
    if d, ok := ag.(agent.SkillDiscoverer); ok {
        skills, _ := d.DiscoverReviewSkills(ctx)
        discoveredNames = namesOf(skills)
    }

    var missing []string
    for _, s := range cfg.Skills {
        if _, ok := builtins[s]; ok           { continue }
        if _, ok := discoveredNames[s]; ok    { continue }
        missing = append(missing, s)
    }
    if len(missing) == 0 { return nil }
    return fmt.Errorf(
        "configured review skill(s) not installed: %s\n"+
        "run `entire review --edit` to reconfigure, or install the plugin and retry",
        strings.Join(missing, ", "),
    )
}
```

Triggered by the *same* error-surfacing pattern as the hooks-installed gate in 1009:

```go
if err := verifyConfiguredSkillsInstalled(ctx, ag, cfg); err != nil {
    cmd.SilenceUsage = true
    fmt.Fprintln(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), err.Error())
    return NewSilentError(err)
}
```

This is the spawn-time backstop for the case the picker can't prevent: user hand-edits `settings.json` and types `/foo:bar` that isn't installed. Without this, `entire review` would spawn, send the composed prompt, and the agent would reply "I don't have that skill" — the silent-failure shape we're explicitly engineering out.

### Edge cases (enumerated with intended behavior)

| Scenario | Behavior |
|---|---|
| No built-ins, no discovered, install hint present (Gemini fresh) | Picker shows two empty-state notes + hint + prompt textarea. User types a Prompt → saves prompt-only config. User leaves blank → final `mergePickerResults` empty-check fires (1009). |
| No built-ins, discovered exists (hypothetical future agent) | Built-in section shows "(none)" note; discovered section populated. Works. |
| Built-ins exist, discovery fails with I/O error | Built-in section populated; discovered section shows "(none)" note (error logged at Debug). Picker still usable. |
| Discovery finds 50+ skills | All rendered. huh scrolls. User scrolls. Acceptable — this is rare. |
| User picks nothing but types prompt | `ReviewConfig{Skills: nil, Prompt: "…"}` saved. `composeReviewPrompt` returns Prompt verbatim at spawn (1009 behavior, unchanged). |
| User picks a discovered skill, then uninstalls the plugin before running `entire review` | Spawn-time re-verification fails. Clear error with remediation, non-zero exit. |
| User's `settings.json` references a skill name outside both built-ins and discovered | Same re-verification failure. |
| 1009's backward-compat break with old `map[string][]string` shape | **Out of scope for this spec.** Assumed resolved in 1009 (either `UnmarshalJSON` migration or atomic land with 993). Noted as a dependency. |

### Testing strategy

**Unit tests (new or extended):**

- `discoverer_test.go` per agent (start: claudecode). Temp dir fixtures:
  - Empty plugin dir → nil, nil
  - Plugin with 1 review skill + 1 non-review skill → 1 result
  - Malformed SKILL.md → skipped, no error
  - Permission-denied subdir → skipped, logged
- `skilldiscovery/match_test.go` — keyword match on name AND description, case-insensitive, every keyword covered
- `review_test.go` extensions:
  - `TestInstallHintSuppressedWhenProvidesAnyMatchesDiscovered`
  - `TestInstallHintShownWhenProvidesAnyEmpty`
  - `TestPickerRendersEmptyBuiltinsAsNote`
  - `TestPickerRendersEmptyDiscoveredAsNote`
  - `TestPickerDedupesBuiltinVsDiscovered`
  - `TestRunReview_MissingSkillAbortsAtSpawn`
  - `TestRunReview_PromptOnlyConfigSkipsSkillVerification`
- Pin the current behavior with a golden test for the composed picker form structure (fields, titles, empty-state notes) — not a full huh render, just the declarative structure

**Integration tests (extend `integration_test/review_test.go`):**

- Fresh Claude Code install, no plugins → picker offers 3 built-ins + install hint; saved config runs without re-verification error
- Claude Code + `/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr` fixture on disk → picker offers built-ins + discovered; install hint for pr-review-toolkit suppressed (because it provides `/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr`); install hint for other packages shown
- Missing-at-spawn: pre-write `settings.json` with `/nonexistent:skill`, run `entire review`, assert stderr match + exit code + marker NOT written

**No E2E tests.** All changes are config-time; no real-agent behavior changes. Existing E2E canary (Vogon) continues to cover the spawn→adopt→commit loop.

### Non-goals (explicit, so reviewers don't ask)

- **Install-on-demand / active install flow** — deferred; the passive hint is the Phase 1 answer.
- **Codex / Gemini discovery implementations** — interface in place, implementations return `nil, nil` until their on-disk layouts are verified against source. Claude Code ships with a real implementation Day 1.
- **Settings shape change** — no change; we build on 1009's `ReviewConfig` shape.
- **Multi-agent parallel spawn, ctrl-o panes, aggregated summary** — Phase 2, separate spec.

---

Section 3 complete. That's the full design:
1. Three-source composition (built-ins + discovery + install hint) with `ProvidesAny` suppression and dedupe.
2. `SkillDiscoverer` as an optional capability interface, per-agent.
3. Keyword-matched discovery, Claude Code Day 1, Codex/Gemini stubbed.
4. Spawn-time re-verification as the silent-failure backstop.

# `entire review` — install-aware picker (Phase 1)

**Status:** design — awaiting implementation plan
**Date:** 2026-04-22
**Author:** Peyton Montei (with Claude Opus 4.7)
**Base branch:** `feat/entire-review` (PR #993 + #1009 stack)

## Problem

The picker in `entire review` (PR #993, hardened in PR #1009) offers a hardcoded list of review skills per agent (`cmd/entire/cli/review.go:126`). Nearly every entry in that list — `/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr`, `/pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer`, `/test-auditor`, `/requesting-code-review`, `/codex:adversarial-review` — requires a plugin install before the agent can resolve it. Users can pick these skills in the picker whether or not they have the plugin installed. When they don't, running `entire review` spawns the agent with a prompt like `Please run /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr`, the agent replies "I don't have that skill," and the session is recorded as a review even though no review ran. Silent failure.

Compounding: Gemini CLI has no built-in review command and no curated entry today, so users with only Gemini installed never see Gemini as a pickable option at all.

## Goals

1. **Eliminate the "skill not installed" silent-failure vector.** Users should not be able to configure a review session around skills that aren't present on disk.
2. **Make discoverability a first-class concern.** Users should see the full set of review-relevant skills actually available to them — built-in and installed plugins alike — and should know where to install more.
3. **Keep the picker scope per-agent** (Phase 1 is single-agent; multi-agent parallel spawn is Phase 2).

## Non-goals

- Install-on-demand / active install flow — passive hints only for Phase 1.
- Changing the settings.json shape — we build on `settings.ReviewConfig` as introduced in PR #1009.
- Multi-agent parallel spawn, ctrl-o panes, aggregated cross-agent summary — Phase 2 spec.
- Full Codex and Gemini CLI discovery implementations — interface is in place Day 1, implementations are stubbed and land in follow-up PRs once their on-disk layouts are verified against source.

## Architecture overview

Per agent, the picker's options list is composed from three sources, rendered in three always-present sections plus a custom-prompt field:

```
 builtins      := curatedBuiltins[agent]                 // hardcoded, guaranteed on disk
 discovered    := agent.DiscoverReviewSkills(ctx)        // scan agent's plugin/skill store
 activeHints   := installHints[agent] − suppressed-by-discovered
```

Final picker form (huh group):

1. **Built-in commands** — multi-select of `builtins`, or a note when `builtins` is empty.
2. **Installed plugin skills** — multi-select of `discovered`, or a note when `discovered` is empty.
3. **Install more** — `huh.NewNote` lines for each unsuppressed entry in `activeHints`. Section omitted entirely if all hints suppressed (so users who have everything installed never see a nag).
4. **Additional instructions (optional)** — `huh.NewText` for a custom prompt. Unchanged from PR #1009.

On picker save, `builtinPicks ++ discoveredPicks` are deduped and stored as `ReviewConfig.Skills`; the textarea content is trimmed and stored as `ReviewConfig.Prompt`. `mergePickerResults` (PR #1009, unchanged) preserves uncurated / external-agent entries the picker couldn't offer.

### Why a capability interface for discovery

`Agent` already uses optional capability interfaces for `Launcher`, `HookSupport`, and others (`cmd/entire/cli/agent/agent.go:258-299`). Adding `SkillDiscoverer` the same way keeps per-agent install-path knowledge local to each agent package. `review.go` never imports `~/.claude/plugins/...` — it asks the agent, "do you have a discoverer, and if so what's on disk?"

## Data model

All new types live either in the agent package (the interface) or in a new `cmd/entire/cli/agent/skilldiscovery/` package (shared helpers + registry data).

```go
// cmd/entire/cli/agent/agent.go
type DiscoveredSkill struct {
    Name        string // e.g. "/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr"
    Description string // from SKILL.md frontmatter `description:` if available, else ""
    SourcePath  string // absolute path — debug logging only; not shown in picker
}

type SkillDiscoverer interface {
    Agent
    // DiscoverReviewSkills scans the agent's on-disk plugin/skill store and
    // returns anything whose name or description matches review-adjacent
    // keywords. Safe on fresh installs — returns nil, nil for missing dirs.
    DiscoverReviewSkills(ctx context.Context) ([]DiscoveredSkill, error)
}
```

```go
// cmd/entire/cli/agent/skilldiscovery/registry.go
type curatedSkill struct {
    Name string
    Desc string
}

type installHint struct {
    Message     string   // rendered as a note line in the picker
    ProvidesAny []string // if any of these names appear in DiscoveredSkills, hint is suppressed
}

var CuratedBuiltins = map[string][]curatedSkill{
    "claude-code": {
        {"/review",          "Review changes and find issues"},
        {"/security-review", "Scan git diff for security issues"},
        {"/simplify",        "Review recent changes for code quality"},
    },
    "codex":      {{"/review", "Review current changes and find issues"}},
    "gemini-cli": {}, // no built-in review command
}

var InstallHints = map[string][]installHint{
    "claude-code": {
        {Message: "Install `pr-review-toolkit` via `claude plugin install entireio/pr-review-toolkit`",
         ProvidesAny: []string{"/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr", "/pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer", "/pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter"}},
        {Message: "Install `test-auditor` via the superpowers plugin",
         ProvidesAny: []string{"/test-auditor"}},
    },
    "codex": {
        {Message: "Install `codex-review-pack` via `codex plugins add …`",
         ProvidesAny: []string{"/codex:adversarial-review"}},
    },
    "gemini-cli": {
        {Message: "Install `gemini-code-review` via `gemini extensions install <url>`",
         ProvidesAny: nil}, // no known skill name to detect; always show
    },
}

var reviewKeywords = []string{
    "review", "audit", "inspect", "critique",
    "assess", "security-scan", "lint",
}
```

**The exact install commands and `ProvidesAny` lists are pinned by real plugin/marketplace metadata at implementation time.** The shape is what's frozen here.

## Discovery algorithm

### Shared contract

`skilldiscovery.Matches(name, description string) bool` — case-insensitive substring match: returns true if `name` or `description` contains any entry in `reviewKeywords`. Shared across all agent implementations so keyword semantics stay consistent.

### Per-agent scan rules

| Agent | Scan root(s) | Skill entry shape | Name format |
|---|---|---|---|
| **claude-code** | `~/.claude/plugins/cache/<marketplace>/<plugin>/<version>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md` + `~/.claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md` | one directory per skill; YAML frontmatter | `/<plugin>:<skill>` for plugin skills, `/<skill>` for user skills |
| **codex** | TBD — verify against `codex-rs/tui/src/...` source for skill/plugin dir layout; current observation is `~/.codex/plugins/<plugin>/` | TBD (SKILL.md or TOML manifest) | `/<plugin>:<skill>` (convention observed in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/codex/AGENT.md`) |
| **gemini-cli** | TBD — verify Gemini extensions layout | per Gemini extension manifest | `/<extension-command>` |

**Implementation ordering:** Claude Code discoverer lands Day 1. Codex and Gemini implementations return `nil, nil` until their on-disk layouts are verified from source; the `SkillDiscoverer` interface and registry entries for built-ins and install hints are in place immediately so the picker renders correctly for all three agents.

### Performance

Discovery runs only inside the picker (first-run or `entire review --edit`). Worst-case scan for a user with 50 plugin skills is ~50 small file reads — well under 100ms on any modern disk. No cache. Simpler is better.

### Graceful failure

`DiscoverReviewSkills` returns `(skills, error)`. All callers treat an error as "found nothing" and log at Debug; discovery never blocks the picker.

- Plugin dir doesn't exist (fresh install, no plugins) → `nil, nil`. Not an error.
- Malformed SKILL.md → skip that skill, log, continue.
- Permission error on a subdir → skip, log, continue.
- Home directory inaccessible → `nil, nil`.

## Picker flow

### Eligibility

An agent appears in the picker if it is:

1. Installed with entire hooks (`GetAgentsWithHooksInstalled`, existing in `review.go:196`), AND
2. Has a non-empty entry in **either** `CuratedBuiltins` **or** `InstallHints`.

Rule (2) is the change: today the filter requires a non-empty `CuratedBuiltins` entry. The new filter is `CuratedBuiltins ∪ InstallHints`, which admits Gemini (empty built-ins but has a hint) without requiring us to curate built-ins we don't actually have.

### Per-agent rendering

```go
for _, agent := range alphabetical(eligibleAgents) {
    builtins    := CuratedBuiltins[agent.Name()]
    discovered, _ := asSkillDiscovererOrNil(agent).DiscoverReviewSkills(ctx) // nil-safe
    discoveredSet := namesOf(discovered)

    // Dedupe: if a "discovered" skill name matches a built-in, drop the
    // discovered row (built-in wins, richer description).
    discovered = filterOut(discovered, func(d DiscoveredSkill) bool {
        return containsBuiltin(builtins, d.Name)
    })

    // Filter install hints via ProvidesAny suppression.
    activeHints := filter(InstallHints[agent.Name()], func(h installHint) bool {
        for _, name := range h.ProvidesAny {
            if _, ok := discoveredSet[name]; ok { return false }
        }
        return true
    })

    form := NewAccessibleForm(huh.NewGroup(
        builtinField(builtins),               // multi-select OR note
        discoveredField(discovered),          // multi-select OR note
        installHintNotes(activeHints),        // 0..n huh.Note; section hidden if 0
        customPromptText(existing.Prompt),    // huh.Text
    ))
    form.Run()

    cfg := settings.ReviewConfig{
        Skills: dedupe(builtinPicks ++ discoveredPicks),
        Prompt: strings.TrimSpace(promptText),
    }
    if !cfg.IsZero() {
        selected[agent.Name()] = cfg
    }
}
```

### Empty-state notes

When a section has no options, substitute the multi-select with a `huh.NewNote`:

- Empty `builtins` → note body: `No built-in review commands in <agent>.`
- Empty `discovered` → note body: `No plugin review skills detected on disk.`
- Empty `activeHints` → section **omitted entirely** (no note, no heading). We don't want a "nothing to install" footer when the user has a rich setup.

## Runtime re-verification

A new guard runs between `selectReviewAgent` and marker write in `runReview`:

```go
if err := verifyConfiguredSkillsInstalled(ctx, ag, cfg); err != nil {
    cmd.SilenceUsage = true
    fmt.Fprintln(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), err.Error())
    return NewSilentError(err)
}
```

```go
func verifyConfiguredSkillsInstalled(ctx context.Context, ag agent.Agent, cfg settings.ReviewConfig) error {
    if len(cfg.Skills) == 0 {
        return nil // prompt-only config — nothing to verify
    }
    builtins := curatedBuiltinNamesForAgent(ag.Name())
    var discoveredNames map[string]struct{}
    if d, ok := ag.(agent.SkillDiscoverer); ok {
        skills, _ := d.DiscoverReviewSkills(ctx)
        discoveredNames = namesOf(skills)
    }
    var missing []string
    for _, s := range cfg.Skills {
        if _, ok := builtins[s]; ok        { continue }
        if _, ok := discoveredNames[s]; ok { continue }
        missing = append(missing, s)
    }
    if len(missing) == 0 {
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf(
        "configured review skill(s) not installed: %s\n"+
        "run `entire review --edit` to reconfigure, or install the plugin and retry",
        strings.Join(missing, ", "),
    )
}
```

This catches the case the picker can't: the user hand-edits `settings.json` and names a skill that isn't on disk, or removes a plugin without updating review config. Without this guard, `entire review` would spawn, compose the prompt, and the agent would respond "I don't have that skill" — restoring the silent-failure shape we're engineering out.

## Edge cases

| Scenario | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Fresh Gemini install, picker shows 0 built-ins + 0 discovered + 1 hint | User can type a custom prompt alone → prompt-only `ReviewConfig`. If they leave blank, `mergePickerResults` emptiness check fires (PR #1009, unchanged). |
| Built-ins present, discovery fails with I/O error | Built-ins section normal; discovered section shows `(none)` note. Error logged at Debug. |
| Discovery finds 50+ skills | All rendered. huh scrolls. No silent truncation. |
| User picks nothing, types prompt | `{Skills: nil, Prompt: "…"}` saved. `composeReviewPrompt` returns Prompt verbatim at spawn (PR #1009, unchanged). |
| User picks a discovered skill, uninstalls its plugin, runs `entire review` | Runtime re-verification fails. Clear error, remediation, non-zero exit. |
| `settings.json` references a skill outside both sources | Same re-verification failure. |
| Multiple install hints for same agent, some suppressed and some not | Unsuppressed hints render; suppressed hints hidden. Section heading shows if ≥1 hint survives. |
| All install hints suppressed (user has everything) | "Install more" section omitted (no heading, no body). |

### Dependency on PR #1009's settings shape compat

PR #1009 changed `EntireSettings.Review` from `map[string][]string` → `map[string]ReviewConfig`. That change has a backward-compat break for any user with the old array-shape persisted (flagged by Cursor Bugbot + Copilot on the PR). **This spec assumes that break is resolved in PR #1009's landing**, either by:

- Adding `UnmarshalJSON` on `ReviewConfig` that accepts both array and object shapes, OR
- Squash-merging PR #993 and PR #1009 together so no released version ever ships the array shape.

The Phase 1 spec does not introduce or remediate that concern; it depends on 1009 being clean before landing.

## Testing strategy

### Unit tests

New file `cmd/entire/cli/agent/skilldiscovery/match_test.go`:

- `TestMatches_NameKeywords` — each entry in `reviewKeywords` matches when appearing in the name.
- `TestMatches_DescriptionKeywords` — each keyword matches when appearing in the description.
- `TestMatches_CaseInsensitive`.
- `TestMatches_NoMatchWhenNeitherFieldContainsKeyword`.

New file `cmd/entire/cli/agent/claudecode/discovery_test.go` (and symmetrical stubs for codex / geminicli):

- Temp dir fixture simulating `~/.claude/plugins/cache/...`:
  - Empty plugins dir → `nil, nil`.
  - Plugin with one review-matching skill + one non-matching → returns one result.
  - Plugin with malformed SKILL.md → skip, log, no error.
  - Plugin with permission-denied subdir → skip, log, no error.
  - Plugin with skill whose name matches a built-in → caller dedupes (tested separately).

Extend `cmd/entire/cli/review_test.go`:

- `TestInstallHint_SuppressedWhenProvidesAnyMatchesDiscovered`.
- `TestInstallHint_ShownWhenProvidesAnyEmpty` (Gemini case).
- `TestPicker_EligibilityIncludesAgentsWithInstallHintEvenWhenBuiltinsEmpty`.
- `TestPicker_DedupesBuiltinVsDiscovered` — if discovery returns a name that collides with a built-in, built-in wins and discovered is dropped.
- `TestRunReview_MissingConfiguredSkillAbortsAtSpawn` — pre-seeded `settings.json` with `/nonexistent:skill`, expects stderr match + non-zero exit + marker NOT written.
- `TestRunReview_PromptOnlyConfigSkipsSkillVerification` — no skills configured but Prompt set, spawn proceeds.

### Integration tests

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (if subagents available) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in plan (not "add validation")
- Exact commands with expected output
- Reference relevant skills with @ syntax
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Plan Review Loop

After completing each chunk of the plan:

1. Dispatch plan-document-reviewer subagent (see plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md) with precisely crafted review context — never your session history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the plan, not your thought process.
   - Provide: chunk content, path to spec document
2. If ❌ Issues Found:
   - Fix the issues in the chunk
   - Re-dispatch reviewer for that chunk
   - Repeat until ✅ Approved
3. If ✅ Approved: proceed to next chunk (or execution handoff if last chunk)

**Chunk boundaries:** Use `## Chunk N: <name>` headings to delimit chunks. Each chunk should be ≤1000 lines and logically self-contained.

**Review loop guidance:**
- Same agent that wrote the plan fixes it (preserves context)
- If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance
- Reviewers are advisory - explain disagreements if you believe feedback is incorrect

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Ready to execute?"**

**Execution path depends on harness capabilities:**

**If harness has subagents (Claude Code, etc.):**
- **REQUIRED:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

- Execute plan in current session using superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching fresh subagent per task, with two-stage review after each: spec compliance review first, then code quality review.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review (spec then quality) = high quality, fast iteration

## When to Use

```dot

    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];

    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];

    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Two-stage review after each task: spec compliance first, then code quality
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture, design, and review tasks**: use the most capable available model.

**Task complexity signals:**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Proceed to spec compliance review.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Prompt Templates

- `./implementer-prompt.md` - Dispatch implementer subagent
- `./spec-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch spec compliance reviewer subagent
- `./code-quality-reviewer-prompt.md` - Dispatch code quality reviewer subagent

## Example Workflow

```

[Read plan file once: docs/superpowers/plans/feature-plan.md]
[Extract all 5 tasks with full text and context]
[Create TodoWrite with all tasks]

Task 1: Hook installation script

[Get Task 1 text and context (already extracted)]
[Dispatch implementation subagent with full task text + context]

Implementer: "Before I begin - should the hook be installed at user or system level?"

You: "User level (~/.config/superpowers/hooks/)"

Implementer: "Got it. Implementing now..."
[Later] Implementer:
  - Implemented install-hook command
  - Added tests, 5/5 passing
  - Self-review: Found I missed --force flag, added it
  - Committed

[Dispatch spec compliance reviewer]
Spec reviewer: ✅ Spec compliant - all requirements met, nothing extra

[Get git SHAs, dispatch code quality reviewer]
Code reviewer: Strengths: Good test coverage, clean. Issues: None. Approved.

[Mark Task 1 complete]

Task 2: Recovery modes

[Get Task 2 text and context (already extracted)]
[Dispatch implementation subagent with full task text + context]

Implementer: [No questions, proceeds]
Implementer:
  - Added verify/repair modes
  - 8/8 tests passing
  - Self-review: All good
  - Committed

[Dispatch spec compliance reviewer]
Spec reviewer: ❌ Issues:
  - Missing: Progress reporting (spec says "report every 100 items")
  - Extra: Added --json flag (not requested)

[Implementer fixes issues]
Implementer: Removed --json flag, added progress reporting

[Spec reviewer reviews again]
Spec reviewer: ✅ Spec compliant now

[Dispatch code quality reviewer]
Code reviewer: Strengths: Solid. Issues (Important): Magic number (100)

[Implementer fixes]
Implementer: Extracted PROGRESS_INTERVAL constant

[Code reviewer reviews again]
Code reviewer: ✅ Approved

[Mark Task 2 complete]

...

[After all tasks]
[Dispatch final code-reviewer]
Final reviewer: All requirements met, ready to merge

Done!
```

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- No file reading overhead (controller provides full text)
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Two-stage review: spec compliance, then code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + 2 reviewers per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip reviews (spec compliance OR code quality)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make subagent read plan file (provide full text instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (spec reviewer found issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- **Start code quality review before spec compliance is ✅** (wrong order)
- Move to next task while either review has open issues

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

Found it. The false positives come from description matching — skills with "review" in their description but not actually review tools:

- `/entire:session-handoff` — description: "inspect recent sessions" (matches `inspect`)
- `/codex:gpt-5-4-prompting` — description: "review, diagnosis, research" (matches `review`)
- `/superpowers:executing-plans` — description: "review checkpoints" (matches `review`)

The legitimate catches (`/superpowers:receiving-code-review`, `/superpowers:requesting-code-review`, `/test-auditor`) all have the keyword in the **name**, not just description.

Also confirmed: **pr-review-toolkit really isn't installed on your disk** (`find ~/.claude/plugins/ -path "*pr-review-toolkit*"` returned nothing). So the install hint is correct — it only *looked* wrong because the false-positive discoveries made it seem like you had plenty of review plugins already.

The fix: **match on name only**. That drops the three false positives and keeps the legitimate ones (because `/pr-review-toolkit:*` has `review` in the plugin prefix, so plugin skills like `silent-failure-hunter` still match via their invocation name).

content.text:
**Addressing your Additional Instructions question first:** Yes, that textarea is from PR #1009. Here's the full story.

**What it is:** A custom prompt override, per-agent. Saved in `.entire/settings.json`:
```json
{
  "review": {
    "claude-code": {
      "skills": ["/review", "/security-review"],
      "prompt": "Focus on data-loss risks first, then run the skills above."
    }
  }
}
```

**How it's used at runtime:** `composeReviewPrompt(cfg)` in `review.go` decides what first message the agent receives:

- **If `prompt` is non-empty:** it's used verbatim.
- **If `prompt` is empty and `skills` is non-empty:** the default template is composed — `"Please run these review skills in order:\n  1. /X\n  2. /Y\n"`.
- **If both empty:** empty string.

**Where it runs:** The composed prompt is (1) written into the pending-review marker so the agent's `UserPromptSubmit` hook records exactly what was asked, and (2) passed to `launcher.LaunchCmd(ctx, prompt)` as the first argument to `claude`/`codex`/`gemini`. When the agent spawns, that text is delivered as the opening user message — same as if you typed it yourself.

So: whatever you type in "Additional instructions" becomes the **literal text Claude/Codex sees at turn one**.

---

Now back to the pr-review-toolkit miss. Found it: **plugins expose slash commands via `commands/*.md` and subagents via `agents/*.md`**, not `skills/*/SKILL.md`. My walker only handled `skills/`. pr-review-toolkit uses `commands/review-pr.md` and `agents/code-reviewer.md` — neither of which I was scanning.

Concrete on your disk:
```
~/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/pr-review-toolkit/unknown/commands/review-pr.md
~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/claude-code-plugins/plugins/pr-review-toolkit/agents/code-reviewer.md
```

And the frontmatter shape differs from SKILL.md:
```
---
description: "Comprehensive PR review using specialized agents"
argument-hint: "[review-aspects]"
allowed-tools: [...]
---
```
No `name:` field — name is derived from the filename (e.g. `review-pr.md` → `/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr`).

**Fix:** extend the Claude Code discoverer to also walk `commands/*.md` and `agents/*.md` per plugin, deriving names from filenames. Applying now.

how do you go back to a section after you click enter, the navigation is weird

That's huh's default navigation, not something we added. Default keybinds in a `huh.Form`:

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `↑` / `↓` (or `j` / `k`) | Move cursor within a list |
| `Space` | Toggle a multi-select option |
| `Enter` | Confirm this field / advance to next |
| `Tab` | Advance to next field |
| **`Shift+Tab`** | **Go back to previous field** |
| `Esc` / `Ctrl+C` | Cancel the whole form |

So **Shift+Tab** is the "go back a section" key you're looking for. Once you've hit Enter on "Built-in commands" and landed on "Installed plugin skills", Shift+Tab returns you to re-toggle built-ins.

If that feels unintuitive (most CLIs don't train users on Shift+Tab), two options for later polish:

1. **Add a "Review your selections" confirmation screen at the end** with an explicit "back" choice — more discoverable, but another step in the flow.
2. **Accept huh's defaults and just document Shift+Tab in the picker hint line** ("Space to toggle, Enter to advance, Shift+Tab to go back, Enter on the final field to save.").
